story_html:
The Fed decides today, and credit didn't wait for the answer. Fed funds are expected to hold at 4.00% at 2pm ET, unchanged from last month's hike — the first since 2023 — with Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference at 2:30pm the part markets will parse hardest (CNBC, Yahoo Finance). Going into the decision, IG OAS (dated Monday 10-26, the usual one-day lag) logged this run's largest flag for a second straight day — z +2.98 — with HY OAS close behind at +2.65 (Dashboard, below). Per §4E, this brief frames the decision rather than calling it in advance: a hawkish hold (language keeping the door open to another hike, continued emphasis on credit conditions) would read as consistent with CL-0052's policy-driven branch; a dovish hold (language leaning toward done-for-now) would read as more consistent with the technical/liquidity branch. Wednesday's statement and Thursday's reconciliation grade the claim — not a forecast made here.

Underneath the Fed story, earnings season split hard today. Boeing fell 10.69% after Tuesday's Q3 report showed its core loss narrowing but still missing the Street's view, with another cut to the 737 delivery forecast (RTTNews). Xylem fell 14.21% to a 52-week low after a Q3 revenue and profit miss and a cut to full-year guidance, with management citing slower conversion of orders to sales and utility customers delaying water-metering purchases (Benzinga, Seeking Alpha, Investing.com) — and the same morning, water-technology peer Pentair rose 12.80% on its own Q3 beat (SEC 8-K, RTTNews). Same sub-industry, same day, opposite directions: that pairing is itself the evidence this was a company-specific story on both sides, not a signal about water-infrastructure demand broadly. Meanwhile the chip and AI-hardware rally that started Monday on Anthropic's IPO filing ran a second day — Dell, Super Micro, Western Digital, Cadence, Coherent, ON Semiconductor and a wide swath of semiconductor names all gained 4-7.5% (Movers/Tier 3, below); this system found no distinct, dated catalyst specific to today beyond that continuation.

Put together, today is one macro test (the Fed) riding on top of a lot of idiosyncratic micro noise. None of the individual earnings moves says anything about the broader economy on its own — that's exactly what the Boeing/Xylem/Pentair pattern shows. The one item without a same-day explanation worth tracking formally is this morning's refiner selloff (Movers, below), logged today as a new conditional claim (CL-0053, Flags) rather than guessed at.
dashboard_interp_html:
Treasury yields barely moved today, which is itself notable hours before the Fed speaks. The 10-year eased 1bp to 4.99% (z +0.99, not flagged; 46th percentile since 1962 but the 83rd of the last 30 years, a real gap marked † — today's lead History-check fact, below). The 3-month bill held at 4.22%, still the dashboard's one flagged Treasury tenor (z +1.60; 52nd percentile since 1981, 70th of the last 30 years) — the bill that will move first and most if today's decision surprises either way. The 2-year rose 2bp to 4.70% (z +1.30, not flagged; 51st percentile since 1976, 80th of the last 30 years, †). The 30-year eased 1bp to 5.30% (z +0.54; 46th percentile since 1977, 81st of the last 30 years, †). Why this matters: the 10-year still prices most fixed mortgages and new bond-fund purchases, and a quiet session like today's means that math is waiting on the 2pm decision, not reacting to anything that already happened.

The curve held its shape: the 2s10s spread (2-year minus 10-year) narrowed 3bp to 29bp, and the 3-month/10-year gap narrowed 1bp to 77bp — both comfortably positive, well clear of the inversion that has historically preceded most recessions (History, below).

Credit stayed in flagged territory into the decision, even as both spreads eased slightly on the day. IG OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to investment-grade companies, dated Monday 10-26) eased 1bp to 0.90% — still the dashboard's largest z-score (z +2.98; 63rd percentile of its own ~3-year record, §4F, no 40-year history here, marked *). HY OAS (the same idea for junk-rated borrowers), also dated 10-26, eased 8bp to 3.30% (z +2.65; 79th percentile of its own ~3-year record, also *) — today's second-largest flag. SOFR, the overnight rate banks pay each other, rose 1bp to 3.93% (z +2.25; 45th percentile since 1954 but the 67th of the last 30 years, † — this print also predates today's decision). The dollar (DXY) firmed to 102.32 (z +1.75 — the dashboard's other flag; 72nd percentile since 1971, 81st of the last 30 years). Fed balance-sheet and TGA readings are last week's H.4.1/DTS release (thin history, carried forward); ON RRP, the nearly-drained shock absorber between them, held near-flat at $0.23B (z −0.52, not flagged). Why this matters: credit spreads, not the Treasury curve, remain this system's best read on whether “tightening” stays orderly through today's decision — both OAS flags held near this run's highs even as the longer-run credit-spread proxy (History, below) still calls investment-grade risk premia historically tight.
history_html:
The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.99% today, a level it first reached Sep 15 and has held on 26 of 30 sessions since; before this run, the last time was Jul 2007. This run's own high (5.31%, Oct 5) is above today's reading — not a new extreme. Today sits at the 46th percentile since 1962 but the 83rd of the last 30 years, a real gap marked † above: unremarkable since the Volcker era, unusually high against just the last three decades.

The real side is more extreme on its narrower record: the 10-year TIPS real yield, 2.66% (dated 10-26), sits at the 99th percentile since 2003; before this run, the last comparable reading was Nov 2008, in the Global Financial Crisis. The Cleveland Fed's longer model (1982+) tempers that to the 80th percentile of the last 30 years, only the 54th since 1982 — high lately, about average on the fuller record.

Credit's own record is short, and it matters today: HY OAS sits at the 79th percentile of its own ~3-year record (§4F, marked *), IG OAS at the 63rd, also *. The 40-year Baa-minus-Treasury proxy — direction and timing only, never magnitude — sits at the 3rd percentile all-time, 2nd of the last 30 years: near four-decade tights. Both true together: real recent widening in the spreads quoted daily, while the longer-run proxy still calls IG risk premia nowhere near historically stressed.

For a client asking if a 5% 10-year and tightening credit mean something's breaking ahead of the Fed: no — six decades call the rate routine, decades of credit history call risk premia tight, not stressed. What's unusual is the pace of this run's own widening — what today's decision will confirm as policy-driven or complicate (CL-0052, above).

concept_title: Broad credit tightening vs. an AI-specific credit story — why Tier 3's weekly depth exists
concept_html: Segments 1-2 built the lens: the Minsky sequence for judging whether a capex boom can fund itself, and vendor financing for telling a growth number apart from a financing-structure artifact. Today's anchor is a limit of this system's own daily data, not a new idea. IG and HY OAS (Dashboard, above) are both flagged this morning — the broadest read this system has: are investors demanding more, generally, to lend to companies. That broad spread can't by itself say whether AI-adjacent borrowers specifically are the ones paying up, or whether this is an economy-wide move that happens to land the same week as the AI buildout's own headlines. Telling those apart needs name-level data a daily pull doesn't carry: the spread on hyperscaler and neocloud bonds specifically, issuance volume, and financing-structure novelty (the Lucent-pattern watch, Unit 7 segment 2). That's exactly why §5 Tier 3 reserves a half-page for Friday depth rather than squeezing issuer-level credit into a daily touch. This morning's broad flag, arriving hours before a Fed decision, is a prompt to watch more closely — not a verdict on the AI-capex cycle specifically.
client_translation: When you hear 'credit markets are tightening,' ask whether that's true for the whole economy or just for one industry -- those call for very different conversations with a client.
client_lens_html:
“The Fed meets today — are rates going up?” Markets are pricing a hold at 4.00% as the most likely outcome, unchanged from last month. The bigger question investors care about is the tone of Chair Warsh's 2:30pm press conference — whether it leaves the door open to another hike or sounds like the Fed is done for now.

“Boeing dropped another 10% — should I worry about my industrials exposure?” Boeing's drop was its own story — a Q3 loss that missed expectations and another cut to its jet-delivery forecast — not a read on industrial companies broadly. The same morning, a different industrial name (Pentair) rose 12.8% on its own earnings beat.

“Chip stocks keep ripping — is this getting ahead of itself?” It's the second straight day of gains on the same AI-demand story, with no new news behind today's move specifically. Worth watching alongside credit spreads (Dashboard, above), which are flagged as tightening even as chip stocks rally — two things that don't usually move the same direction for long.
